passage: "Suraj, you're teaching Class 4 now, so listen to your old Vaibhav Chacha for a minute. Years ago I had a boy in my class, bright as a lamp. Around Diwali he changed. He snapped at his friends over nothing. He put his head on the desk every afternoon. He stopped playing kabaddi, which he used to love, and every week he said his stomach hurt. The other teachers said, 'Cranky phase. He'll grow out of it.' But it didn't pass. Weeks, then two months. One day I asked him gently, 'What's it like inside, these days?' He said, 'Grey, Sir.' Just that. Grey. I called his parents that same evening, and they took him to a doctor who helped. Children don't say 'I feel low,' Suraj. They show it. Watch for the change that stays."

qa.q: What game did the boy stop playing?
qa.a: Kabaddi, which he used to love.

qa.q: What did the boy's answer 'Grey, Sir' reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: It revealed that he felt low and flat inside, even though he had only shown it as crankiness and tiredness.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav Chacha advise Suraj to watch for?
qa.a: A change in a child that stays, because children show low mood through behaviour instead of saying it.

qa.q: How did the other teachers see the boy's behaviour, and why was that risky?
qa.a: They saw a cranky phase he'd grow out of, which could have left his lasting sadness unnoticed.

grounding: An elder recalls a child whose low mood showed as crankiness, tiredness, lost interest in play and stomach aches, and a lasting change that got attention.

passage: With the new baby home and both parents on night shifts at the hospital, nobody had much time for Nirmala, ten. The flat was full of crying and tired whispers. When Rashmi Masi came to help, she noticed at once. Nirmala snapped at her little cousin over a pencil. She lay on the sofa after school, too tired to change. Her dance bag hadn't moved from the corner in weeks. Twice she said her head hurt. "She's just jealous of the baby," her mother sighed. But Rashmi sat with Nirmala on the balcony and asked, "Is everything a bit heavy lately?" Nirmala nodded and cried silently. That night Rashmi told her sister, "This has gone on too long to be a phase." The next day, between shifts, they took Nirmala to the doctor together.

qa.q: Where had Nirmala's dance bag been lying?
qa.a: In the corner, not moved in weeks.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when Rashmi asked about things being heavy?
qa.a: She felt low and relieved to be asked; she nodded and cried silently.

qa.q: What choice did Rashmi make that changed things?
qa.a: Instead of accepting it as jealousy, she gently asked Nirmala, then told her sister the lasting change needed a doctor.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's mother see the behaviour, and why?
qa.a: She saw it as jealousy of the baby, perhaps because she was exhausted from night shifts and caring for the newborn.

grounding: It shows a child whose low mood looks like crankiness, tiredness, tearfulness, lost interest and aches, with a relative noticing a lasting change that deserves attention.

passage: Noa used to be first on the netball court in their Cape Town school. Now she missed practice three weeks running. She lay in bed until noon on weekends and scrolled until three in the morning, not even really seeing what was on the screen. "You coming to Thabo's braai?" her friend texted. She didn't answer. Later she wrote in her notes app: I don't feel anything. I'm useless anyway. Her mother called it an attitude problem at first. Then she found Noa sitting in the dark bathroom, not crying, just staring. "This isn't you being lazy, is it?" her mother said softly, sitting on the floor beside her. Noa shook her head. The next morning her mother took the day off and drove Noa to the family doctor.

qa.q: How late did Noa scroll at night?
qa.a: Until three in the morning.

qa.q: What did Noa's note 'I don't feel anything. I'm useless anyway' show about her inner state?
qa.a: It showed she felt numb and worthless, not simply bored or lazy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how her mother responded?
qa.a: She stopped calling it an attitude problem, sat beside Noa gently, and took her to the family doctor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Noa doesn't answer about the braai?
qa.a: Thabo might feel confused or ignored, not knowing that Noa is struggling with something serious.

grounding: It shows a teenager who sleeps and scrolls for hours, drops friends and sport and feels numb and worthless, treated as a health matter rather than laziness.

passage: At the residential school, Tushar's bed by the window stayed made up for Sunday chess club, but he never went anymore. He slept through breakfast bell. He stopped going to the common room when his friends watched matches. His roommate Nilesh heard the warden call it laziness. "Get up, Tushar, this attitude won't work here." But one night Nilesh heard Tushar whisper into his pillow, "I'm useless. I'm just a waste of a seat." Nilesh sat up. "Hey. You're not useless. But I think something's really wrong, and it's not your fault." The next morning he walked Tushar to the school counsellor's room before assembly, and waited on the bench outside. The counsellor called Tushar's parents that afternoon and arranged a visit to the doctor.

qa.q: What did Tushar used to go to on Sundays?
qa.a: Chess club.

qa.q: What did Tushar's whisper reveal about how he saw himself?
qa.a: It revealed that he felt worthless, calling himself useless and a waste of a seat.

qa.q: Which choice by Nilesh helped most?
qa.a: He took Tushar's words seriously, said it wasn't his fault, and walked him to the counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: How might the warden see Tushar differently after the counsellor's call?
qa.a: The warden might see that Tushar's sleeping and withdrawal are signs of a health problem, not laziness or attitude.

grounding: It shows a teenager who oversleeps, drops friends and hobbies and feels worthless, which is not laziness but a health matter for a counsellor and doctor.

passage: Dear Kamal, I'm writing this because every time I try to talk, one of us walks away. For months you've been in your room with the door shut. You snap at me when I ask about school. On Sunday I shouted, "Just cheer up, what's wrong with you?" I'm sorry. I was frightened, and it came out as anger. I've been reading, and talking to your class teacher. I think you might be carrying something heavy, and that is not your fault. I'm not going to lecture you. I'd like to listen, whenever you're ready, even if it's just to sit together. I've also booked an appointment with a counsellor for Thursday. Will you come with me? I'll wait in the car if you want. I love you, stubborn boy. Amma (Urmila)

qa.q: When is the counsellor appointment?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when she shouted 'Just cheer up'?
qa.a: She felt frightened, and it came out as anger.

qa.q: What change in approach does Urmila offer Kamal?
qa.a: She apologises, promises to listen instead of lecture, and has arranged professional support with the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading this letter compared with being shouted at?
qa.a: He may feel less blamed and more cared for, which could make him more willing to talk or go on Thursday.

grounding: It shows a parent who sees her teen pull away and snap, feels frightened and angry, and turns to concern, listening and professional support instead of telling him to cheer up.

passage: "You want to know how it started, Anand? I'm Bhupen, and I'll tell you straight. I was angry. My son Tushar was fifteen. Overnight, it felt like, he stopped talking to us. Door shut. Plate left full. If I asked about cricket, which he'd loved, he snapped, 'Leave me alone!' I thought, this boy is being rude to his own father. I shouted back more than once. I felt helpless, and helpless turned into angry. Then my wife showed me his notebook, full of 'I'm tired' written over and over. That stopped me cold. That night I knocked, sat on the floor by his bed and said, 'I'm not angry. I'm worried about you. Tell me when you can.' He didn't talk much. But the next week he let me take him to a counsellor. We're still going, together."

qa.q: What was written over and over in Tushar's notebook?
qa.a: I'm tired.

qa.q: What made Bhupen feel angry at first?
qa.a: He felt helpless when his son pulled away and snapped, and the helplessness turned into anger.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Bhupen approached his son?
qa.a: Seeing the notebook, he knocked, sat on the floor and spoke with worry instead of blame, then took him to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Tushar have experienced his father's shouting before the change?
qa.a: He may have felt more alone and misunderstood, pushing him further behind the shut door.

grounding: A father recalls feeling helpless and angry as his son pulled away and snapped, then approaching with concern, listening and arranging professional support.

passage: "Here's the thing people don't get. I never missed a class. Not one. I'm Lalit, and in my third year I was top of the attendance list and completely empty inside. I'd sit in lectures and hear nothing. At night I was exhausted but couldn't sleep. And the thought that kept coming back was: everyone would be happier if I wasn't around. I didn't say it to anyone. I was scared and ashamed of it. One evening my friend Ira asked, 'You've been somewhere else for weeks. What's going on?' And I just said it. The thought, out loud. Ira didn't panic or lecture. She said, 'Thank you for telling me. You're not a burden. We're going to get help tonight.' She stayed with me, called the campus helpline with me, and walked me to the counsellor first thing next morning. That's why I'm here talking to you."

qa.q: What list was Lalit at the top of in third year?
qa.a: The attendance list.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the thought that kept coming back?
qa.a: Lalit felt scared and ashamed of it and kept it secret.

qa.q: What was the turning point that got Lalit help?
qa.a: Lalit spoke the thought out loud to Ira, who stayed, called the campus helpline with Lalit that night and went to the counsellor next morning.

qa.q: How did Ira's response make it easier for Lalit?
qa.a: Ira stayed calm, thanked Lalit, said Lalit was not a burden and acted at once, so Lalit felt safe rather than judged.

grounding: It shows a young adult who keeps attending class but feels empty, exhausted and hopeless and thinks others would be better off without them, and how speaking up and professional help matter.

passage: I'm Payal, and I share a flat with Anirban. From the outside he was fine. He went to the office every day, ironed his shirts, smiled at our landlord. I didn't notice much, except that his dinner plate often went back to the fridge untouched, and he slept all Sunday. Last Friday he was washing up and said, very flatly, "Honestly, you'd all be better off without me." I don't know exactly what was in his head. But I didn't let it go. I turned off the tap and said, "I heard that. I'm staying right here with you." We sat on the kitchen floor. I asked if he was safe tonight, and he said he wasn't sure. So I called his brother, and we rang a helpline together. His brother came over and stayed. Next morning we went with him to a doctor.

qa.q: What did Anirban say while washing up?
qa.a: Honestly, you'd all be better off without me.

qa.q: What does Anirban saying he wasn't sure if he was safe suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hopeless and was struggling far more than his daily routine showed.

qa.q: Which of Payal's choices mattered most that night?
qa.a: Payal took his words seriously, stayed with him, asked about his safety, called his brother and a helpline, and went with him to a doctor.

qa.q: How might Anirban's brother have felt getting Payal's call?
qa.a: He likely felt shocked and scared but grateful Payal called, so he could come and stay with Anirban.

grounding: A flatmate sees a young adult who keeps working but hardly eats, sleeps a lot and says others would be better off without him, and gets him help the same night.

passage: "Dilnaz, got a minute? Just us." "If it's about the rent, I'll pay Monday." "It's not the rent. You've skipped dinner all week. You cancelled the film, and the birthday." "I'm busy, Sharmila." "And yesterday you said, 'What's the point of any of it.' I keep thinking about that." "It was a joke. Don't lecture me." "I won't. I'm not here to fix anything. I just miss you, and I'm worried." A long silence. Dilnaz picks at her sleeve. "Everything's just... heavy. All the time." "Okay. Thank you for telling me. I'm staying right here." "I don't know what to do." "Would you see the campus counsellor? I can book it with you, right now. I'll walk you there." "...Only if you come." "I'm coming."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz cancel, according to Sharmila?
qa.a: The film, and the birthday.

qa.q: Why does Dilnaz say 'Don't lecture me'?
qa.a: She seems to feel resentful and defensive, expecting to be judged for the way she has been acting.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's choices helped Dilnaz open up?
qa.a: Sharmila checked in privately, named what was noticed, promised not to lecture, and simply stayed.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see Sharmila's offer to walk with her?
qa.a: She may feel less alone and more able to go, since she agrees only if Sharmila comes.

grounding: A friend notices missed meals, cancelled plans and dark remarks, checks in privately, listens and stays present, and gently encourages professional help.

passage: I'm Tenzin. Last year my roommate Jagdish slowly disappeared in front of me, and I almost didn't notice. First it was meals. He'd say he'd eaten, but his plate stayed clean in the rack. Then he pulled out of the trek we'd planned for months. Then the remarks: "Nothing I do matters anyway." I laughed the first time. I'm not proud of that. The third time, I shut the door and sat on his bed. "You don't have to talk. But I've noticed you're not eating, and I'm worried about you." He didn't say anything for a long time. Then he said, "I'm so tired of feeling like this." I didn't try to fix it. I just stayed. Over the next week I kept asking gently, and in the end he let me go with him to the college doctor.

qa.q: What trip did Jagdish pull out of?
qa.a: The trek they had planned for months.

qa.q: What does Jagdish saying 'I'm so tired of feeling like this' show?
qa.a: It shows he had been struggling with low feelings for a long time and was worn out by them.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do after the third remark that helped?
qa.a: Tenzin shut the door, spoke privately, named the worry, stayed without trying to fix it, and later went with him to the doctor.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when Tenzin laughed at the first remark?
qa.a: He may have felt unheard and more alone, which could have made it harder to speak up.

grounding: A roommate recalls noticing missed meals, cancelled plans and dark remarks, checking in privately, staying present and encouraging professional help.

passage: "Eshaan, sit. You're worried about your friend Kunal, na? Let me tell you about my friend Suresh, forty years ago. He stopped coming to the tea stall. Stopped laughing. Said he had no reason to get up. Everyone told him, 'Cheer up, yaar.' That only made him hide. I didn't tell him to cheer up. I said, 'Come walk with me to the post office.' Ten minutes. Next day, I brought dal and rice and we ate on his step. Small things. Then I helped him book a doctor's appointment, and I went along. But hear this too. I had my own job, my own family. I couldn't carry him alone. When he once said something that scared me, I told his brother that same evening. That wasn't betrayal, beta. That was care. Suresh is still my friend today." Yogesh Chacha refilled Eshaan's glass of water.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh invite Suresh to walk?
qa.a: To the post office, for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh tell Suresh's brother when Suresh said something frightening?
qa.a: Yogesh was worried about Suresh's safety and knew he couldn't carry him alone.

qa.q: What small actions does Yogesh describe that Eshaan could try?
qa.a: Short walks, a shared meal, helping book a doctor's appointment and going along, without demanding cheerfulness.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when everyone said 'Cheer up, yaar'?
qa.a: He probably felt misunderstood and pushed away, which made him hide more.

grounding: An elder recalls supporting a friend with small doable actions, not demanding cheer, helping book an appointment, respecting his own limits and involving family over safety.

passage: It was the worst possible week: Jasleen had two exams and a project due, and only two hundred rupees left till her scholarship came. But Rekha, her flatmate, hadn't left her bed in three days. Jasleen didn't say, "Smile, it's not that bad." She said, "Walk with me to the chai stall? Five minutes." Rekha came, silent, in a hoodie. That evening Jasleen cooked one pot of dal and they ate it on the floor. She sat beside Rekha while Rekha booked a slot at the campus clinic. Then Rekha whispered, "Sometimes I don't want to wake up." Jasleen's heart jolted. She held Rekha's hand and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm calling your sister now, okay?" Rekha nodded. Her sister came that night. Jasleen asked their friend Mehak to sit with Rekha the next evening, so she could sleep before her exam.

qa.q: How much money did Jasleen have left till her scholarship came?
qa.a: Two hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Rekha whispered she sometimes didn't want to wake up?
qa.a: She felt shocked and scared; her heart jolted, but she stayed calm and held Rekha's hand.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's choices protected both Rekha and herself?
qa.a: She called Rekha's sister at once over safety, and asked Mehak to sit with Rekha so she could rest before her exam.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Jasleen didn't tell her to smile?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt accepted as she was, which made small steps like the chai walk and the clinic booking possible.

grounding: It shows a supporter who offers small actions like a walk and shared meal, does not demand cheerfulness, helps book an appointment, involves family over safety and minds her own limits.

passage: March. Chandrika used to love her job designing book covers. Now she opened a file, stared at the blank screen for an hour and closed it. Mangoes, music, her Sunday calls with Kashish: nothing tasted of anything. Each evening she lay on the bed thinking, I'm lazy. I'm letting everyone down. It will always be like this. April. Kashish came over without calling. "You sound like a recording of yourself. Will you see someone?" Chandrika cried, then let Kashish sit beside her while she booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist. The doctor she saw later explained treatment options. June. It hadn't vanished. But one morning she finished a rough sketch before lunch. That evening Kashish brought mangoes, and Chandrika noticed, with surprise, that they tasted sweet.

qa.q: What did Chandrika design at work?
qa.a: Book covers.

qa.q: What did Chandrika believe about herself each evening in March?
qa.a: She believed she was lazy, letting everyone down, and that it would always be like this.

qa.q: What was the turning point in April?
qa.a: Kashish came over and asked her to see someone, and Chandrika booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the moment the mangoes tasted sweet?
qa.a: Kashish would likely see it as a sign that Chandrika's heaviness is slowly lifting with support and treatment.

grounding: It shows a young professional who loses pleasure, cannot start tasks and feels guilty, whose depression feels permanent but begins to lift with support and treatment.

passage: "Vasudha, close the laptop for a minute. I saw you staring at that report for an hour. I know that stare. I had it at your age. I was twenty-five, new job, everything I'd wanted. And I stopped enjoying anything. Not my food, not my music, not even my niece's laugh. I would sit down to work and my hands just wouldn't start. Then I'd feel so guilty I'd sit there till midnight, getting nothing done. The worst part was the voice that said, 'This is who you are now. Forever.' It was lying. I didn't know that yet. My sister dragged me to a doctor. Then I saw a therapist every week for months, and the doctor treated me too. Slowly, colour came back. I'm not your doctor, Vasudha. But I'll help you find one, today if you like." Ganga pushed a cup of tea across the desk.

qa.q: How old was Ganga on stopping enjoying anything?
qa.a: Twenty-five, in a new job.

qa.q: What does Ganga mean by saying the voice 'was lying'?
qa.a: Ganga means the feeling that it would last forever was not true; with treatment, it lifted.

qa.q: What offer does Ganga make that could be a turning point for Vasudha?
qa.a: Ganga offers to help Vasudha find a doctor, even that same day.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel hearing this from a senior colleague?
qa.a: Vasudha may feel less ashamed and less alone, and more hopeful that her own heaviness can lift.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls losing pleasure and motivation with guilt at twenty-five, and how treatment from qualified clinicians lifted a depression that felt permanent.

passage: Monday. In the queue at the stationery shop, Dolma's heart suddenly started pounding so hard she could hear it. The shelves tilted. Her hands tingled. Something terrible is happening, she thought, I'm going to collapse. She ran outside and gripped the railing. Ten minutes later it faded, leaving her shaky and confused. Two weeks later. She hadn't gone back to that shop. She took the long way to tuition to avoid the market. She'd started skipping the crowded school canteen. Her world was getting smaller, and she knew it. The Saturday after. She told her friend Sunaina everything, and Sunaina came with her to tell her mother. At the clinic the doctor checked her carefully and explained what had happened in her body. "It's frightening, but it passes. We can work on the fear of the next one."

qa.q: Where did Dolma feel the sudden wave of fear?
qa.a: In the queue at the stationery shop.

qa.q: What did Dolma think was happening during the attack?
qa.a: She thought something terrible was happening and that she was going to collapse.

qa.q: What turning point came on the Saturday?
qa.a: She told Sunaina, who went with her to tell her mother, and a doctor explained what happens in her body.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt hearing Dolma's story?
qa.a: Sunaina may have been worried for Dolma, and glad Dolma trusted her enough to share it.

grounding: It shows a teenager with a sudden pounding heart, dizziness and a sense of doom that passes, whose fear of the next attack starts to shrink her life.

passage: "Jatin, you said your heart went crazy in the exam hall, like you were dying? Sit. Your Tarun Chacha knows that feeling. I was sixteen, at the cinema with friends. In the middle of the film my heart started hammering. I couldn't breathe properly. Everything went far away, like looking down a tunnel. I was sure something terrible was happening. I ran out into the lobby. After a few minutes it slowly passed, and I sat there shaking. After that, I stopped going to the cinema. Then I stopped going to cricket in case it happened in front of everyone. My life got smaller and smaller, all out of fear of the next one. Your Dadi finally took me to a doctor. He explained it was panic, frightening but not dangerous, and it passes. That changed everything. So tomorrow, we'll tell your parents and see the doctor together."

qa.q: Where was Tarun Chacha when his first attack happened?
qa.a: At the cinema with friends, in the middle of the film.

qa.q: What was Tarun afraid of after the first attack?
qa.a: He was afraid it would happen again in front of everyone, so he feared the next one.

qa.q: What does Tarun Chacha suggest Jatin do next?
qa.a: Tell his parents tomorrow and see the doctor together.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel hearing that his uncle had the same experience?
qa.a: He may feel less alone and less frightened, knowing it passed for his uncle and could be understood.

grounding: An uncle recalls a sudden wave of fear with a pounding heart and a sense of something terrible, which passed but whose fear made his life smaller.

passage: I'm Manjula, and I still remember the day Lalit sat down on the corridor floor outside the exam hall. His face had gone grey, and he was gasping. "I can't breathe. Something's wrong. I'm dying." A crowd started to gather. I asked them to give us space. Then I sat down next to him, close but not touching, and spoke slowly. "I'm here. This is a wave of panic. It's horrible, but it will pass. Breathe out slowly with me." I didn't argue with him or say, "You're fine." I just kept saying it would pass, and it did, after a few long minutes. When it happened again the next month, I told him gently, "I think you should see a doctor or a counsellor about this." He went. I went with him.

qa.q: Where did Lalit sit down when the panic started?
qa.a: On the corridor floor outside the exam hall.

qa.q: What did Lalit believe was happening during the attack?
qa.a: He believed something was wrong and that he was dying.

qa.q: Which of Manjula's choices helped Lalit most in the moment?
qa.a: Manjula cleared the crowd, sat close without touching, spoke slowly, and kept reminding him it would pass.

qa.q: How might the gathering crowd have made things worse for Lalit?
qa.a: Being crowded and stared at could have made him feel more trapped and frightened.

grounding: It shows a calm companion who stays close, speaks slowly, reminds the person it will pass, does not crowd or argue, and later encourages professional help.

passage: Coach's note, district meet Before the 400m final, Tejas was found in the changing room, doubled over, gasping and shaking. He said, "My heart, something's badly wrong." His teammates were crowding round, all talking at once. What I did: I asked the others to wait outside. I sat a little distance from him and spoke slowly. "Tejas, I'm here. This is panic. It's frightening, and it will pass." He said, "No, it won't." I didn't argue. I kept my voice low and breathed slowly where he could see me. After a few minutes his breathing eased. Afterwards I told his parents. If it happens again, I've suggested they see a doctor or a counsellor together. He didn't run the final. He's running next month. - Rajni, athletics coach

qa.q: Where was Tejas found before the 400m final?
qa.a: In the changing room, doubled over, gasping and shaking.

qa.q: What was Tejas afraid of during the attack?
qa.a: He was afraid something was badly wrong with his heart.

qa.q: What did Rajni do when Tejas said 'No, it won't' pass?
qa.a: Rajni didn't argue, but kept a low voice and breathed slowly where he could see.

qa.q: How might Tejas's teammates have affected him by crowding round?
qa.a: All talking at once, they may have made the panic worse by crowding him.

grounding: A coach's note shows staying close, speaking slowly, saying it will pass, not arguing or crowding, and afterwards encouraging a doctor or counsellor if it recurs.

subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: Dear Arohi, You asked why I keep saying no to plans. I owe you the real answer. Since the panic attack on the metro in March, I've been avoiding things. First the metro. Then crowded lectures. Then the big exam hall. I sit near doors. I check where the exits are. I'd rather miss the concert with you than risk it happening in the crowd. But I've started seeing a psychologist, and it's helping. She explained what my body is doing in an attack: my alarm system going off by mistake. My heart speeds up, I breathe too fast, I feel dizzy, and it's scary but not dangerous. Understanding that has taken away half the fear. Last week I did two metro stops with her plan. Next month, maybe the concert? Your friend, Irfan

qa.q: Where did Irfan's first panic attack happen?
qa.a: On the metro in March.

qa.q: Why has Irfan been saying no to plans?
qa.a: Irfan fears having another panic attack in a crowd, so has been avoiding things.

qa.q: What turning point is helping Irfan face the fear?
qa.a: Seeing a psychologist, understanding what the body does in an attack, and trying small steps like two metro stops.

qa.q: How might Arohi have seen Irfan's refusals before this letter?
qa.a: Arohi might have thought Irfan didn't want to spend time together, not that fear was behind it.

grounding: It shows a young adult avoiding trains, crowds and exams in case panic strikes, and how understanding the body and professional guidance reduce the fear.

subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: "So, Wasim, since you asked. The first one happened in the university library, and for a year after that I organised my whole life around not having another one. I'm Siddharth. I stopped taking the train home and paid for expensive cabs I couldn't afford. I sat every exam near the door, and I dropped a subject because its exam was in the huge hall. My world shrank to my room, the canteen and one corridor. What changed? My sister made me see a counsellor. She drew me a diagram of what happens: the body's alarm fires, adrenaline, fast heart, fast breathing, the feeling of doom, and then it drops. It always drops. Once I understood that, the attacks lost their power. Now I take the train again, one stop at a time."

qa.q: Where did Siddharth's first attack happen?
qa.a: In the university library.

qa.q: What was Siddharth afraid of for a year after the first attack?
qa.a: Siddharth was afraid of having another one, so organised life around avoiding it.

qa.q: What turning point helped Siddharth take the train again?
qa.a: Seeing a counsellor who explained what happens in the body, which took away the attacks' power.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's sister have felt watching Siddharth's world shrink?
qa.a: She was likely worried, which is why she pushed Siddharth to see a counsellor.

grounding: It shows a young adult avoiding trains and exams in case panic strikes again, and how understanding the body and professional guidance reduce fear.
